source_url: cite: Kurzweil, Ray. The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology. New York: Viking, 2005. Chapter One, The Six Epochs, section The Singularity Is Near
quote: With both the hardware and software needed to fully emulate human intelligence, we can expect computers to pass the Turing test, indicating intelligence indistinguishable from that of biological humans, by the end of the 2020s.
claim_summary: Computers will pass the Turing test, with intelligence indistinguishable from humans, by the end of the 2020s.
timeline_text: by the end of the 2020s
definition_note: Turing test pass; intelligence indistinguishable from that of biological humans
notes: timeline_year 2029 read from 'end of the 2020s'. Wording checked against an online text copy of the book on archive.org (item kurzweil-ray-the-singularity-is-near), which looks like an unauthorised upload, so the book is cited rather than linked. Publication month September 2005 from search results, not checked against the publisher.

quote: I set the date for the Singularity—representing a profound and disruptive transformation in human capability—as 2045.
claim_summary: Kurzweil sets 2045 as the date of the Singularity, a profound and disruptive change in human capability.
definition_note: Singularity, not AGI; the same Q&A says 'We'll have both the hardware and software to recreate human intelligence by the end of the 2020s'
notes: Question-and-answer page on the book's official site, undated; the Kurzweil Library reprints the same dialogue (thekurzweillibrary.com/dialogue-a-conversation-on-the-singularity) and says it comes from The Singularity Is Near (2005). source_type interview because it is a question-and-answer format written for the book.

quote: We'll have sufficient hardware to recreate human intelligence pretty soon. We'll have it in a supercomputer by 2010. A thousand dollars of computation will equal the 10,000 trillion calculations per second that I estimate is necessary to emulate the human brain by 2020. The software side will take a little longer.
claim_summary: Hardware able to recreate human intelligence will exist in a supercomputer by 2010 and for $1,000 by 2020; the software will take a little longer.
timeline_text: The software side will take a little longer
definition_note: Hardware able to emulate the human brain (supercomputer by 2010, $1,000 by 2020); a timeline for computing power, not for human-level AI itself
notes: Ubiquity magazine interview (vol. 7 issue 1, 11-17 January 2006), read in the excerpt reposted to the Humanist discussion list; the ACM original (ubiquity.acm.org/article.cfm?id=1117663) returned 403. Speaker's own words in a published interview, so treated as primary.

quote: At the end of the 2020s, we will have both the hardware and software to create human levels of intelligence. This includes emotional intelligence, which is really the cutting edge of intelligence, in a machine.
claim_summary: By the end of the 2020s there will be the hardware and software to create human-level intelligence, including emotional intelligence, in a machine.
timeline_text: At the end of the 2020s
definition_note: human levels of intelligence, including emotional intelligence
notes: Interview by Sander Olson, first published on CRNano.org 9 February 2006 and reprinted on KurzweilAI.net 10 February 2006. timeline_year 2029 read from 'end of the 2020s'.

quote: I've made the case that we will have both the hardware and the software to achieve human level artificial intelligence with the broad suppleness of human intelligence including our emotional intelligence by 2029
claim_summary: Human-level AI, with the breadth of human intelligence including emotional intelligence, will be achieved by 2029.
definition_note: human level artificial intelligence with the broad suppleness of human intelligence including emotional intelligence
notes: secondhand; Ubergizmo quoting the BBC story "Machines 'to match man by 2029'" on Kurzweil's talk at the American Association for the Advancement of Science meeting in Boston, February 2008. The BBC original (news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/7248875.stm) could not be fetched, nor its archive.org copy.

quote: For starters, I said that we would be able to reverse-engineer the brain sufficiently to understand its basic principles of operation within two decades, not one decade, as Myers reports.
claim_summary: Kurzweil corrects a reported date: understanding the brain's basic principles of operation will take two decades, not one.
timeline_text: within two decades, not one decade
definition_note: Understanding the brain's principles of operation, which he treats as the route to human-level AI; not AGI itself
notes: computed: 2010 + 20; also: possibility. Reply to biologist PZ Myers's post "Ray Kurzweil does not understand the brain"; corrects a press report of his Singularity Summit 2010 talk. Code judged: the date is for a step toward human-level AI rather than for AGI.

quote: So when a computer does reach human levels, which I believe will happen by the end of the 2020s, it will be able to go out on the Web and read billions of pages as well as have experiences in online virtual worlds.
claim_summary: Replying to Paul Allen's argument that the Singularity is far off, Kurzweil holds that computers will reach human levels by the end of the 2020s.
timeline_text: by the end of the 2020s
definition_note: human levels of intelligence; human-level pattern recognition combined with computer speed
notes: also: timeline. Published in Technology Review as "Don't Underestimate the Singularity" (October 2011); the Kurzweil Library copy is dated 20 October 2011. The technologyreview.com URL tried returned 404. Coded possibility because the essay argues the brain is understandable enough to be rebuilt, against Allen; the date is secondary. timeline_year 2029 read from 'end of the 2020s'.

quote: This is about typical for the state of the art in chatbots, and I've seen better.
claim_summary: Kurzweil rejects the claim that the Eugene Goostman chatbot passed the Turing test, calling it typical of current chatbots, while keeping his 2029 date for a valid test.
timeline_text: I specified the 2029 date in my 1999 book
definition_note: valid Turing test: longer than five-minute conversations, no restricted persona such as a 13-year-old non-native speaker
notes: also: timeline. Kurzweil's own post. Stance judged: he dismisses the current claim but remains expectant about a genuine pass by 2029; the same post predicts a period of premature claims that will be debunked.

quote: The median view of AI practitioners today is that we are still several decades from achieving human-level AI. I am more optimistic and put the date at 2029, but either way, we do have time to devise ethical standards.
claim_summary: In an essay arguing AI dangers can be managed, Kurzweil puts human-level AI at 2029, earlier than the median expert view of several decades.
timeline_text: put the date at 2029
definition_note: human-level AI
notes: also: timeline. Op-ed by Kurzweil in TIME, "Don't Fear Artificial Intelligence". Coded post_agi because the essay is about managing risk; source_type blog used for a signed opinion piece (no op-ed type in the codebook).

quote: I've stuck with my 2029 prediction, which is now a median view and there is a growing group of people who think I am too conservative.
claim_summary: Kurzweil keeps his 2029 date for human-level machine intelligence, says it is now a median view, and notes many think it too conservative.
timeline_text: I've stuck with my 2029 prediction ... a growing group of people who think I am too conservative
definition_note: human-level intelligence in a machine
notes: Kurzweil's foreword to Martine Rothblatt's book Virtually Human; the Kurzweil Library dates it 1 March 2016. The book itself may have been published earlier (2014, not checked).

quote: One is 2029, which is when computers will pass a valid Turing test, meaning they'll be indistinguishable from human intelligence in a conversation.
claim_summary: Asked why the Singularity is set for 2045, Kurzweil names 2029 as the year computers pass a valid Turing test.
timeline_text: One is 2029
definition_note: 2029 = valid Turing test pass (indistinguishable from human intelligence in conversation); the same answer explains 2045, the Singularity, as when nonbiological intelligence is a billion times all human intelligence
notes: Playboy interview published 19 April 2016, reprinted in the Kurzweil Library.

quote: 2029 is the consistent date I have predicted for when an AI will pass a valid Turing test and therefore achieve human levels of intelligence. I have set the date 2045 for the 'Singularity' which is when we will multiply our effective intelligence a billion fold by merging with the intelligence we have created.
claim_summary: Kurzweil restates 2029 for a valid Turing test pass and human-level intelligence, and 2045 for the Singularity.
timeline_text: 2029 is the consistent date I have predicted
definition_note: 2029 = valid Turing test pass, which he equates with human levels of intelligence; 2045 = Singularity, multiplying effective intelligence a billion-fold by merging with AI
notes: Statement made "in a communication to Futurism" around SXSW 2017. The Kurzweil Library dates the Futurism story March 2017; the Futurism page shows only 'Updated Oct 16, 2017'.

quote: By 2029, computers will have human-level intelligence.
claim_summary: On stage at SXSW 2017, Kurzweil says computers will have human-level intelligence by 2029.
definition_note: human-level intelligence
notes: secondhand; Fox News (16 March 2017) reporting Kurzweil's SXSW session in Austin (interviewers Shira Lazar and Amy Kurzweil). Futurism carries the same quote. No recording or transcript of the session was found; a web search for it could not be run because the search budget ran out.

quote: We're not quite there, but we will be there, and by 2029 it will match any person.
claim_summary: On Joe Rogan's podcast Kurzweil says AI is not yet at human level but will match any person by 2029.
timeline_text: We're not quite there, but we will be there
definition_note: match any person
notes: secondhand; also: capability_now. Business Today (13 March 2024) reporting Joe Rogan Experience episode 2117. archive.org copies of the episode have no transcript or captions; no published transcript found.

quote: Human-level intelligence generally means AI that has reached the ability of the most skilled humans in a particular domain and by 2029 that will be achieved in most respects.
claim_summary: Kurzweil says AI will reach the ability of the most skilled humans in most respects by 2029, perhaps still trailing in a few skills.
timeline_text: by 2029 that will be achieved in most respects
definition_note: ability of the most skilled humans in a particular domain; 'in most respects' by 2029, may still lag top humans in a few skills such as Oscar-winning screenplays or deep new philosophical insights
notes: secondhand; PC Gamer story (8 July 2024, via Yahoo Tech) quoting the Guardian interview of 29 June 2024 (theguardian.com/technology/article/2024/jun/29/ray-kurzweil-google-ai-the-singularity-is-nearer), which the fetch tool could not reach. Hedge: 'in most respects'. Same story quotes 'We're going to expand intelligence a millionfold by 2045'.

quote: But that's now starting to look like a conservative view
claim_summary: Kurzweil says his 2029 date for AGI now starts to look conservative, implying it could come sooner.
timeline_text: now starting to look like a conservative view
definition_note: AGI matching or surpassing human capabilities across a wide range of cognitive tasks (the outlet's wording); same interview: the Singularity is 'where we no longer have control of AI'
notes: BBC Science Focus interview by Alex Hughes. Hedge toward an earlier date. The 2029 date is stated by the outlet in the sentence before the quote. Medium confidence because the definition is the outlet's.

quote: Basically, it will be able to do what an expert in every field can do, all at the same time, and we're not quite there yet, but we will be there by 2029.
claim_summary: Kurzweil defines AGI as doing what an expert in every field can do at once, says it is not here yet, and keeps 2029.
timeline_text: we're not quite there yet, but we will be there by 2029
definition_note: what an expert in every field can do, all at the same time
notes: also: capability_now, definition. TWiT Intelligent Machines episode 810 transcript (0:07:53). Asked whether he wants to adjust the date he said: 'Well, there's no reason for me to adjust it. I mean, I said 2029 in 1999.' (0:11:12). Same episode puts the Singularity, merging with AI, at 2045.

quote: Hinton was saying that he did not expect A.I. to be achieved for decades. “No sooner than 2070,” he said. “I am in the camp that is hopeless.”
claim_summary: Told Nick Bostrom, in a reporter's hearing, that he did not expect (human-level) AI for decades, no sooner than 2070, and that he was pessimistic about how it would be used.
timeline_text: No sooner than 2070
definition_note: "A.I." in a conversation with Bostrom about superintelligence; reporter's word, not defined
notes: also: post_agi. Said at the Royal Society machine learning conference where Hinton gave the keynote (event page path dated 2015/05); article published 2015-11-16. Same occasion: 'there is not a good track record of less intelligent things controlling things of greater intelligence.' Stance judgment: far-off timing (skeptical) but explicitly pessimistic about the outcome, so alarmed. Earliest dated timeline in his record.

quote: While Google uses AI in its search engines to learn how to return smarter query results, Hinton predicts it still will take more than five years before machines possess human-level abilities.
claim_summary: A trade-press article reports Hinton predicting that machines are still more than five years from human-level abilities.
timeline_text: more than five years
definition_note: human-level abilities
notes: secondhand; computed: 2016 + 5 (lower bound only). Paraphrase by MediaPost (Laurie Sullivan), which does not say where Hinton said it; original not found because web search was unavailable (hinton-047). source_type is the type of the unknown original, best guess interview.

quote: I think computers will eventually surpass the abilities of the human brain, but different abilities will be surpassed at different times. It may be a very long time before computers can understand poetry or jokes or satire, as well as people.
claim_summary: Asked how soon machines will surpass the human brain, says they eventually will, ability by ability, but some abilities like understanding jokes may take a very long time.
timeline_text: eventually ... It may be a very long time
definition_note: surpassing the abilities of the human brain; uneven by ability
notes: also: timeline. Interview question: 'How soon will machines be able to compete with – and surpass – the human brain? Or has Google's AlphaGo already proven that time is now?' Frame judgment: asked 'how soon' but the answer is about eventual possibility, no date.

quote: I do believe deep learning is going to be able to do everything, but I do think there's going to have to be quite a few conceptual breakthroughs.
claim_summary: Says deep learning will be able to replicate all of human intelligence, given several conceptual breakthroughs and a massive increase in scale; no date.
definition_note: all of human intelligence (interviewer's framing)
notes: Interview with Karen Hao, MIT Technology Review (EmTech 2020). Asked if breakthroughs would let deep learning approximate all human intelligence: 'Yes.' Stance judgment: confident it will happen (expectant), though 'breakthroughs needed' could read as skeptical.

quote: Until quite recently, I thought it was going to be like 20 to 50 years before we have general-purpose AI. And now I think it may be 20 years or less
claim_summary: Says he used to expect general-purpose AI in 20 to 50 years and now thinks it may be 20 years or less.
timeline_text: may be 20 years or less
definition_note: general-purpose AI
notes: also: self_improvement, post_agi. computed: 2023 + 20 (upper bound). CBS Saturday Morning interview with Brook Silva-Braga. Same interview: 'might be' close to computers coming up with ideas to improve themselves; human extinction 'not inconceivable'; worrying now is reasonable 'even though it's not going to happen in the next year or two'. Stance judgment: hedged worry, before his Google exit; cautious rather than alarmed.

quote: The idea that this stuff could actually get smarter than people — a few people believed that... But most people thought it was way off. And I thought it was way off. I thought it was 30 to 50 years or even longer away. Obviously, I no longer think that.
claim_summary: Says he used to think AI smarter than people was 30 to 50 years or more away and obviously no longer thinks so.
timeline_text: I thought it was 30 to 50 years or even longer away. Obviously, I no longer think that.
definition_note: smarter than people
notes: New York Times interview by Cade Metz, 'The Godfather of A.I.' Leaves Google and Warns of Danger Ahead (https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/01/technology/ai-google-chatbot-engineer-quits-hinton.html). nytimes.com could not be fetched; quote read in the EA Forum linkpost reproducing the article's quotes. Primary words, copy source, hence medium. The '...' replaces the reporter's 'he said'. Gives a past estimate and rejects it without a new number.

quote: I have suddenly switched my views on whether these things are going to be more intelligent than us. I think they're very close to it now and they will be much more intelligent than us in the future.
claim_summary: Says current large language models are very close to human intelligence now and will be much more intelligent than people.
timeline_text: very close to it now
definition_note: more intelligent than us
notes: also: post_agi. Interview with Will Douglas Heaven, MIT Technology Review, the day after his Google exit was reported; same interview: 'How do we survive that?'

quote: Scott Pelley: You believe that ChatGPT4 understands? Geoffrey Hinton: I believe it definitely understands, yes. Scott Pelley: And in five years' time? Geoffrey Hinton: I think in five years' time it may well be able to reason better than us.
claim_summary: Says GPT-4 definitely understands and that in five years AI may well reason better than people.
timeline_text: in five years' time it may well be able to reason better than us
definition_note: reasoning better than humans
notes: also: capability_now, self_improvement, post_agi. computed: 2023 + 5. CBS 60 Minutes, Scott Pelley. Same interview: 'we may have things more intelligent than us'; systems 'might escape control... by writing their own computer code to modify themselves'; takeover 'a possibility'. Frame judgment: timeline and capability_now both prominent; the dated claim chosen.

quote: However, I think it might have been unfortunate in that we're going to get superintelligence faster than I thought, and I wish I'd thought about safety earlier.
claim_summary: At a Nobel week press conference in Stockholm, says superintelligence is coming faster than he thought; the reporter adds that he thinks it could arrive in five to 20 years.
timeline_text: faster than I thought; (reporter) next five to 20 years
definition_note: superintelligence (surpassing even the smartest humans)
notes: also: post_agi. computed: 2024 + 5 to 2024 + 20. Canadian Press report (article dated 2024-12-08) of a Stockholm press conference the reporter attended; the quote is direct, the five-to-20-year range is the reporter's paraphrase, hence medium. Same piece: humanity may have to 'worry seriously about how we stay in control.'

quote: A year ago, he believed it would be five to 20 years before the arrival of AI that can surpass human intelligence in every domain. Now, he says 'there's a good chance it'll be here in 10 years or less.'
claim_summary: Says there is a good chance AI surpassing humans in every domain arrives in 10 years or less, shorter than his five-to-20-year estimate a year earlier.
timeline_text: there's a good chance it'll be here in 10 years or less
definition_note: superintelligence: AI that can surpass human intelligence in every domain
notes: secondhand; also: post_agi. computed: 2025 + 10 (upper bound). Business Insider write-up (on Yahoo, 2025-04-28) of the CBS Saturday Morning interview with Brook Silva-Braga aired 2025-04-26. The CBS article (https://www.cbsnews.com/news/godfather-of-ai-geoffrey-hinton-ai-warning/) was read but carries no timeline line, only the tiger-cub analogy and a 10-20% takeover risk. A 'good chance' is not a stated probability, so not prob_by_year.

quote: Most experts think sometime between five and twenty years ... I used to say thirty to fifty years. Now, it could be more than twenty years, or just a few years.
claim_summary: At the Ai4 conference in Las Vegas, says most experts put AGI between five and twenty years away and that he now thinks it could be anywhere from a few years to more than twenty.
timeline_text: could be more than twenty years, or just a few years
definition_note: AGI (article's term)
notes: secondhand; also: post_agi. MacDailyNews (2025-08-14) carrying Forbes's (Ron Schmelzer, 2025-08-12) direct quotes from the Ai4 talk; forbes.com returned 403. The '...' joins two quotes the article prints together, not certain they were consecutive in the talk. Fox Business (2025-08-13) paraphrased the same remarks as 'as little as just a few years away'; TechNews.tw as 'within 10 years'. Stance judgment: the timing words are a wide hedge (cautious) though the talk was about control risk.

quote: Noting that predictions about when superintelligence would be reached used to range from 30 to 50 years, Hinton said, "Then those predictions dropped to maybe 10, maybe 20 years."
claim_summary: At a briefing for members of Congress, says superintelligence estimates have fallen from 30-50 years to 10-20 and that many researchers now say it may be about one year away; says AIs are now designing better AIs.
timeline_text: Maybe one year, but not much more than one year
definition_note: superintelligence
notes: secondhand; also: self_improvement. computed: 2026 + 1. Türkiye Today (2026-09-18) citing NBC News on a briefing for members of Congress led by Senator Bernie Sanders on 2026-09-16; original NBC report not found (hinton-063). Same report quotes 'Maybe one year, but not much more than one year' (attributed to what many researchers now say) and that AIs are 'now designing better AIs'. Briefing, not formal testimony; source_type testimony is the nearest fit.

quote: As yet, we haven’t figured out how to build a machine that fully comprehends the concept of “dinner”, much less something as abstract as “harm” or “protection.” ... A.I. has a long way to go before laws as abstract as Asimov’s could realistically be encoded in software.
claim_summary: Today's AI cannot grasp even everyday concepts, so it is a long way from machines that could follow abstract ethical rules.
notes: also: post_agi; New Yorker online essay 'Moral Machines'. newyorker.com could not be reached, so the text was read from a PDF copy of the article on a Manchester University course page. Borderline: about machine understanding in general, not AGI by name.

quote: New York University professor Gary Marcus, CEO of Geometric Intelligence, says Hawking and Musk have a point, but the existential threat they fear is still many decades off and people face somewhat different threats from AI in the nearer term.
claim_summary: The threat from superintelligent machines that Hawking and Musk warn of is many decades away; nearer-term AI risks matter more.
timeline_text: still many decades off
definition_note: threat from superintelligent machines, not AGI as such
notes: secondhand; paraphrase of Marcus's Wall Street Journal essay 'Artificial Intelligence Isn't a Threat-Yet' (Dec 2014) as reproduced on David Luckham's blog. wsj.com could not be reached and the follow-up search could not run (search budget exhausted). Same page: Marcus says 'superintelligent' machines are unlikely to arrive soon.

quote: I don't think the robots are anywhere near as clever as Hal, and aren't going to be for at least thirty or fifty years or something like that.
claim_summary: Machines as clever as HAL, the computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey, are at least 30 to 50 years away.
timeline_text: at least thirty or fifty years or something like that
definition_note: as clever as Hal (HAL 9000), i.e. human-level general AI
notes: computed: 2016 + 30 = 2046, 2016 + 50 = 2066; 'at least' makes both years lower bounds. Edge conversation (edited transcript of an interview).

quote: I still feel like we're actually no closer to the moon, where the moonshot is intelligence that's really as flexible as human beings. We're no closer to that moonshot than we were four years ago.
claim_summary: Deep learning has not brought AI any closer to intelligence as flexible as a person's.
definition_note: intelligence as flexible as human beings
notes: also: timeline (same interview: 'some people are hysterical about it, thinking that real AI is around the corner and it probably isn't'). Interview for the Flux podcast published as a transcript on TechCrunch.

quote: I present ten concerns for deep learning, and suggest that deep learning must be supplemented by other techniques if we are to reach artificial general intelligence.
claim_summary: Deep learning on its own will not reach AGI; other techniques are needed.
notes: abstract of 'Deep Learning: A Critical Appraisal'. Treats AGI as reachable by a different route.

quote: But you know, we're pretty far from that right now. AlphaGo can play very well on a 19×19 board but actually has to be retrained to play on a rectangular board.
claim_summary: Current deep learning systems are far from general AI; they cannot transfer even simple skills.
notes: Answer to the question 'deep learning can't really reach general AI because it's missing deep understanding.' Interview about the book Rebooting AI. Same interview: 'A hundred years from now, AI will warrant our trust—and maybe sooner' (about trustworthiness, not AGI, so not coded as a timeline).

quote: I seriously doubt it. In truth, we are still a long way from machines that can genuinely understand human language, and nowhere near the ordinary day-to-day intelligence of Rosey the Robot
claim_summary: Deep learning will not do everything; machines are still far from understanding language or everyday intelligence.
definition_note: ordinary day-to-day intelligence (Rosey the Robot)
notes: magazine essay 'Deep Learning Is Hitting a Wall'; replying to Hinton's 2020 claim that deep learning 'is going to be able to do everything'.

quote: Being realistic, 7 years might well not be enough to (a) invent those tools (if they are don't already exist) and (b) take them from the lab into production.
claim_summary: Seven years, to 2029, is probably too short to reach AGI; he offers Musk a bet that AI will not pass at least three of five tests in 2029.
timeline_text: 7 years might well not be enough
definition_note: bet test: in 2029 one AI passing at least three of five tasks (understand a movie, understand a novel, cook in an unfamiliar kitchen, write 10,000 lines of bug-free code from a spec, formalize proofs)
notes: computed: 2022 + 7 = 2029. Reply to Elon Musk's prediction of AGI by 2029; the post sets out the bet ('I offered to place a bet on it'). timeline_year is the year he doubts, not an expected date.

quote: My own skepticism has limits. I do think we will eventually reach AGI (artificial general intelligence), and quite possibly before the end of this century.
claim_summary: AGI will eventually be built, quite possibly before 2100.
timeline_text: quite possibly before the end of this century
notes: also: possibility; dialogue with Grady Booch, who argued AGI will not come in our lifetimes. Later in the dialogue Marcus asks 'Why be so sure we can't do that in the next 75 years?' Cuts against his skeptic reputation.

quote: When we get to artificial general intelligence, maybe let's say it's 50 years, that really is gonna have, I think, profound effects on, on labor.
claim_summary: Told the US Senate that AGI might be about 50 years away and will have profound effects on jobs when it comes.
timeline_text: maybe let's say it's 50 years
notes: incidental; also: timeline; computed: 2023 + 50; found by the Altman trace (altman-033), quote re-checked against the transcript by the coordinator; stance could be read as cautious

quote: Let's not dumb down our standards, and wind up with a bunch of machines we can't rely on, just so that big tech can prematurely declare victory, when there is plenty of work left to do.
claim_summary: AGI is not imminent; current machines fall short and claims of near AGI lower the bar.
definition_note: argues Shane Legg's 2023 bar (beating typical human performance on cognitive tasks) is weaker than earlier definitions
notes: also: timeline, definition (post title: 'No, Virginia, AGI is not imminent'). Reply to Shane Legg.

quote: But there is zero justification for claiming that the current technology has achieved general intelligence.
claim_summary: Large language models are not AGI, despite claims that AGI is already here.
definition_note: My bar for AGI is a machine that can do the cognitive tasks that people can typically do.
notes: Reply to Blaise Agüera y Arcas and Peter Norvig, 'Artificial General Intelligence Is Already Here'.

quote: Skeptical of this, I offered Musk a $1 million bet that AGI superior to the smartest individual humans would not arrive by the end of 2025
claim_summary: AGI smarter than the smartest people will not arrive by the end of 2025; he offered Musk a $1 million bet on it.
timeline_text: would not arrive by the end of 2025
definition_note: AGI superior to the smartest individual humans
notes: timeline_year is the year by which he says it will not arrive. Same bet as his 2024-04-09 open letter ('$10 million says we won't see human-superior AGI by the end of 2025'), treated as one occasion.

quote: If you read his manuscript, please read it for his concerns about our underpreparedness, not for his sensationalist timelines.
claim_summary: Rejects the forecast of AGI by 2027 as sensational but says we are badly unprepared for AGI whenever it comes.
timeline_text: AGI whenever it comes
notes: also: post_agi; reply to Leopold Aschenbrenner's AGI-by-2027 forecast. Same post: 'woefully underprepared for AGI whenever it comes'.

quote: Both of us agree that the achievement of 8 out of 10 of these tasks would be strong evidence for the G (General) in Artificial General Intelligence having been achieved.
claim_summary: Bet with Miles Brundage on whether AI can do 8 of 10 hard tasks by the end of 2027; Marcus takes the side that it will not.
timeline_text: by the end of 2027
definition_note: 8 of 10 listed cognitive tasks
notes: Co-written with Miles Brundage in the third person. Stakes: $2,000 from Marcus against $20,000 from Brundage; the post tells readers not to infer Gary's beliefs from the odds, so no probability is recorded.

quote: We will not see artificial general intelligence this year, despite claims by Elon Musk to the contrary.
claim_summary: AGI will not arrive in 2025.
timeline_text: will not see artificial general intelligence this year
notes: timeline_year is the year by which he says it will not arrive.

quote: Gary Marcus stands by his prediction that we will not see AGI in 2025, and regrets that Elon Musk didn't take his million dollar bet.
claim_summary: Repeats that AGI will not arrive in 2025.
timeline_text: will not see AGI in 2025
notes: Written in the third person on his own newsletter. Reply to Sam Altman's 'We are now confident we know how to build AGI'. timeline_year is the year by which he says it will not arrive.

quote: And even though I highly doubt AGI will arrive in three years, I can't absolutely promise you it won't happen in 10.
claim_summary: AGI by 2028 is very unlikely, but he cannot rule it out within ten years.
timeline_text: highly doubt AGI will arrive in three years, I can't absolutely promise you it won't happen in 10
